title: Koliko je sati?
theme: Clocks and daily rhythm across Bosnia and Herzegovina
reviewerNotes: Revised for BiH geographic diversity (Travnik, Una/Bihać, Neum) and accurate Travnik sahat-kula art. ready for human review.
storyBeat: Emir teaches Ana the time, then shows that Bosnia’s rhythm is bigger than one city: Travnik’s sahat-kula, Una mornings near Bihać, and weekend dreams of Neum.

vocabulary: Ask the clock question Koliko je sati?
Name jutro, podne, popodne, and večer
Use danas, sutra, and the weekdays from ponedjeljak to nedjelja
grammar: Ask and answer the hour with sat and sati
Use danas and sutra for today and tomorrow
Reuse familiar present-tense frames from earlier lessons.
culture: See sahat-kule clock towers in towns across Bosnia and Herzegovina, not only Sarajevo
Visit Travnik under Vlašić, the Una near Bihać, and Neum on the Adriatic

grammar.title: Koliko je sati?
grammar.explanation: Hold this as a spoken pattern, not a grammar grid. Ask the time with Koliko je sati? Answer with a number from Lesson 3 plus sat or sati. Say Jedan je sat for one o’clock. For two through four you will often hear sati. Keep the chunk short and clear.

examples.bosnian: Osam je sati. / U osam sati.
examples.english: It is eight. / At eight o’clock.

grammar.title: Danas and sutra
grammar.explanation: Learn the usable chunk first; full tables can wait. Danas means today. Sutra means tomorrow. Pair them with a weekday. Say Danas je petak. Say Sutra je subota. You can also place plans with Sutra u deset sati.

grammar.title: Weekdays. chant the week
grammar.explanation: Keep this as a sayable line rather than a paradigm list. Learn the seven days as a list. The words are ponedjeljak, utorak, srijeda, četvrtak, petak, subota, and nedjelja. Watch the special letters in srijeda and četvrtak.

culture.title: Time across Bosnia: Travnik’s sahat-kula
culture.body: Ottoman Bosnia left sahat-kule (clock towers) in many towns, not just Sarajevo. Emir’s photo today is Travnik: a stone sahat-kula under the cliffs of Mount Vlašić, once a seat of Ottoman viziers. Sarajevo’s tower by Gazi Husrev-beg’s mosque was famous for lunar prayer time. Travnik keeps a different skyline under the mountain. Day rhythm changes with place too. There is misty jutro on the Una near Bihać, bright inland popodne, and večer plans for Neum on Bosnia’s short Adriatic coast. Learning to ask Koliko je sati also means learning where in the country that hour belongs.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson A: Ask the time
lessonBlocks.body: Drill Koliko je sati? Then answer with Lesson 3 numbers. Say Pet je sati. Say Osam je sati. Say Deset je sati. Say Jedan je sat. Add place chunks such as U osam sati kod Amire and U dvanaest sati for podne. Emir flips a postcard of Travnik’s sahat-kula while Ana practices. The same question works in every Bosnian town. Ana still says Kasno je! when she is late for kahva.
tips: Reuse numbers one through twelve from Lesson 3.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson B: Days and the week’s plan
lessonBlocks.body: Chant the weekdays twice. Then build real lines. Say Danas je petak. Say Sutra je subota. Mark the parts of day with jutro, podne, popodne, and večer. Emir sketches a wider week on a napkin and teases subota by the Una and nedjelja dreams of Neum. For now they stay in Sarajevo, but sutra always points somewhere on the map of Bosnia and Herzegovina. End with one plan. Say Sutra u deset sati, kod Amire!
tips: Pair danas or sutra with a weekday.
Četvrtak and srijeda need careful letters.

conversation.title: Koliko je sati, Emire?
conversation.setting: Outside Amira’s, late afternoon. Ana checks her phone; Emir shows a postcard of Travnik’s clock tower under Vlašić.

lines.speaker: Emir
lines.bosnian: Da. Sutra u deset sati ovdje.
lines.english: Yes. Tomorrow at ten o’clock here.

lines.speaker: Amira
lines.bosnian: Jutro za kahvu. Subota za rijeku!
lines.english: Morning for coffee. Saturday for the river!

funFacts.title: Travnik and Vlašić
funFacts.body: Travnik has its own central-Bosnia weight on the map. It was a major Ottoman administrative centre under Mount Vlašić. Its sahat-kula still marks the town’s skyline. When you practice clock time, remember that Bosnian history is not only a Sarajevo footnote.

funFacts.title: Many sahat-kule
funFacts.body: Clock towers appear in towns across Bosnia and Herzegovina. Sarajevo and Travnik are only two of the places that kept a sahat-kula. Sarajevo’s tower is often remembered for once tracking lunar prayer time. That detail roots the question Koliko je sati in local history, not only in a classroom drill.

funFacts.title: Una mornings near Bihać
funFacts.body: In the northwest, the Una River runs clear past Bihać. Locals talk about jutro on the river with real affection. The feeling matches the love Sarajevo keeps for a slow kahva. Different place, same habit of starting the day gently.

funFacts.title: Neum touches the sea
funFacts.body: Bosnia and Herzegovina has a short Adriatic coastline at Neum. A plan for sutra can mean salt air, not only mountain towns. That matters when you practice danas and sutra as real calendar words. Time phrases feel more alive when they can point to an actual coast.

civicContext.title: A country with almost no sea door of its own
civicContext.body: Bosnia and Herzegovina has almost no independent door to the sea. Its only coastline is the short stretch at Neum, and much Adriatic freight still depends on access through Croatia. Croatia’s Pelješac Bridge, opened in 2022, connects Croatian territory around Neum, while traders in Bosnia and Herzegovina still face foreign customs regimes rather than a full national deep-water port system. A weekend plan for the coast therefore sits inside a larger dependence on a neighbor for much of the country’s maritime trade access.
